(Place of publication: India) Oṃ.

Salutations to Śrī Sundaragaṇapati. [The Ritual for Worship for the Sake of Others] (ṚE-30482). [F1a mentions the title of the text and the name of the scribe]. [The Ritual for Daily Worship by Araśūrī Tyāgarāya Guru].
[Written by one's own hand] | (F1b is blank) The Ritual for Worship for the Sake of Others (F1a,
first line)

Having approached the presence of the Kṣetrapāla and performed the worship of the gateway, one should offer the bath and other consecrations, as well as worship, food offerings, incense, lamps, and the *arghya* water; then one should pray: "O Lord Kṣetrapāla, for the sake of protecting all people on this earth, [grant] the staff that is the limb of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva."

Saying "Give it to me," he takes the staff [marked] with the goad-seal (*aṅkuśamudrā*) and other signs, approaches the door of the bedchamber, and— having caused the songs and instrumental music of the *rudragaṇikās* to be played at the side of the door for the purpose of opening the eyes of Śiva and Śakti—
and having opened the door-panel by means of the worship of the door, he enters within after warding off the three obstacles, using the *arghya* water with the *astra-mantra*.
Oṃ Ca.

Having sprinkled the curtain for concealment (*tirodhānapaṭa*) with the *avṛta* mantra, worshipped it with the *varman* mantra, and placed it above the throne, one should sprinkle the image with the *astra* mantra, discard the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*), and give water with the *astra* mantra for the purification of the feet and hands; then, for the sake of bathing, one should sprinkle [the deity] with the water of the *arghya* offering using the root mantra (*mūla*).
Having adorned [the image] with various garlands, perfumes, and floral wreaths,

having worshipped it with the root-mantra and the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and the water for honor (*arghya*), one should place the deity upon a palanquin— without the *Śakti*— and,
accompanied by all musical instruments and attendants, approach the vicinity of the *liṅga*. Then, upon its head, with a flower and the *Udbhava-mudrā*, [one should perform the rite].

Having joined [the deity] to the *liṅga* and established the image (*mūrti*) in its proper place, one should perform the purification of the bath while standing upon the tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*) for the purpose of worship.
(4th line) One should carry out the purification of the bath.
Having sprinkled the ground with *arghya* water and demarcated a square area with the *astra-mantra*,
one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Goddess of the Earth (*bhūmidevī*) by means of her seat (*āsana*) and other rites, followed by meditation (*dhyāna*).
The goddess has two arms and two eyes, is adorned with a crown containing a casket, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is embellished with all ornaments.

Having meditated thus, having worshipped with the Heart and Weapon [mantras], and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and the water for honor (*arghya*), this is the purification of the site (*sthalaśuddhi*). Having washed the conch, the vessel for *arghya*, the vessel for water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the vessel for water for the feet (*pādya*), the flowers, and the other vessels with the Weapon mantra, having established them with the Heart mantra, having gazed upon them, and having rendered them nectarine (*amṛtīkṛtya*), one should fill the *vardhanī* and the conch vessel with water using the Root mantra, and [fill] the *vardhanī* with the Śiva mantra.
Having worshipped [the deity], having honored him with the limbs (*aṅga*),
having consecrated [the water] with mantras, and having worshipped the *astra-mantra* below, one should display the *liṅga-padma-mudrā*.

Having performed the five purifications (*pañca-śuddhi*) of the conch-water, having worshipped it with the root mantra, and having consecrated it eleven times with the ten-syllable seed mantra, one should display the great *astra-mudrā* below and offer incense and lamps.
Having given [that], and having sprinkled the ritual substances with that water, one should prepare the vessels for the special *arghya*, the *pādya*, and the *ācamanīya*.
Within those—

Having placed the aforementioned substances [into the vessels], one should worship the *arghya* water with the *astra*, *brahma*, and *aṅga* mantras, and consecrate it. One should worship the *pādya* vessel with the *hṛdaya* mantra and consecrate it seven times with the *praṇava*. One should consecrate the *ācamanīya* vessel with the ten-syllable mantra, consecrating it that many times, and then display the five mudrās, beginning with the *dhenu* mudrā, followed by incense and the lamp.
(7th line) Having given [the offerings], there is the purification of the substances.

For the purpose of meditating upon the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*), one should place scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) on the palm of the right hand with the root mantra, while using the left hand— (F2b, 1st line)

Having prepared the perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having performed the rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) up to the consecration as nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) with the left hand, one should worship the seat consisting of Dharma and the other [qualities] and the Form (*mūrti*).
Then, having applied the root-mantra and the limb-mantras (*brahmāṅga*), and having meditated upon [the deity] in the form of light, one should deposit [it] upon the head with the *Śiva-mantra*.

Having gazed with a gracious disposition and divine vision upon two cubits, one should contemplate the Hand of Śiva. On the western side, having prepared a square measuring one cubit with rice grains, one who has studied the Vedas should, in the center, create grid compartments by means of lines numbering twelve (the sun), within five equal pathways.
Therein, having set aside the first rule and having purified the second row, and having likewise inscribed the previously mentioned number of blisses, one should write:

"Obeisance to the square of the principle of Śiva" in the central square; "Obeisance to the square of the principle of Sadāśiva" in the east; "Obeisance to the square of the principle of Vidyā" in the south.

Salutation to the square of the *puruṣa-tattva* in the north. Salutation to the square of the *kāla-tattva* in the west. (F3a, first line) Salutation to the square of the *īśvara-tattva* in the southeast. Salutation to the square of the *pāda-tattva* in the southwest. Salutation to the square of the *niyati-tattva* in the northwest. (second line)

In the northeast, [one should say]: "Obeisance to the square of the *prakṛti*-tattva. Having thus worshipped the squares and offered incense and lamps, one should surround the nine vessels with the *astra* mantra and wash them with the *hṛdaya* mantra.

Having sprinkled [the area] with the Astra-mantra and protected it with the Varma-mantra, having offered incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*), one should place the vessels in the center of the enclosure.

In the middle: *oṃ hāṃ supratiṣṭhitapātrāya namaḥ*. In the east: *oṃ hāṃ suśāntapātrāya namaḥ*. In the south: *tejovatpātrāya namaḥ*. In the north: *ratnodakapātrāya namaḥ*. In the west: *amṛtātmakapātrāya [namaḥ]*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ namaḥ" in the northeast [saying] "Oṃ namaḥ to the vessel of the Unmanifest," and having worshipped from the southeast to the northwest [saying] "Oṃ namaḥ to the vessel consisting of nectar," and having adorned [them] with perfumes and other offerings, one should worship the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra in the regions to be meditated upon within the central vessel.
Having worshipped Gaṇapati, Ṣaṇmukha, Nandin, and Mahākāla from the east to the north of that [central vessel], and having honored the four Vedas in the intermediate directions,

and having offered incense, lamps, and *arghya*, one should fill the central vessel with milk using the mantra "āpyāyasva," and [place] curd in the southern [vessel] using the mantra "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam."
In the east, place *śukram asi* and ghee; in the north, *sāvitrā* and cow’s urine; in the west, *gandhadvārā* and cow dung; in the northeast, *devasya tvā* and *kuśodaka*.

From the southeast to the northwest, having established the substances of oil, flour, *āmalaka*, and turmeric with the *astra-mantra*, and having arranged the *kūrca*-grass, sprouts, gems, and coconut, one should sprinkle them with the *puṇyāha* water, followed by the *kṣīra* and other liquids ending with *kuśodaka*.

With the mantra *īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām*, one consecrates five vessels with five, four, three, two, and one mantra respectively; having invoked [the deities] and displayed the mudrās as prescribed, one offers the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamp, and water for honor (*arghya*). Having worshipped the other vessels with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and displayed the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*), one consecrates the milk and other substances ending with *kuśa* water, and the oil and other substances ending with turmeric, using the root mantra, the Brahma-mantras, the *vyāhṛtis*, the ten seed-syllables, and the *bhikrama* mantra.

Having combined the substances contained in the five vessels starting from the east into the central vessel, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times. Having performed the protection (*avakuṇṭhana*) of the directions and their presiding deities, one should cover [the vessel] three times with the mantra *mā nastoke tanaye*. Then, lifting the tip of the nose while uttering the *nāda* with both the left and right hands, one should establish and worship it with the root mantra; this is the *pañcagavya*.

Then, having prepared a mound of rice with *śāli* grains in the western part for that five-nectar (*pañcāmṛta*) offering, and having arranged nine squares in the center, one should worship the four squares starting from the southeast (*āgneyī*).
In the central square: *oṃ hāṃ namas* to the cell of the earth element (*pṛthivī-tattva*). In the east: *oṃ hāṃ namas* to the cell of the water element (*ap-tattva*). In the south... [F4b, line 1]

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the square of the fire element (*vahnitattva*). In the west: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the square of the air element (*vāyutattva*). In the north: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the square of the space element (*vyomatattva*). Having worshipped thus, having wrapped the vessels with thread, having washed them with the *astra-mantra*, and having offered incense and a lamp with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should place the vessels in their respective squares. In the center: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel of the fragrance element (*gandhatattva*). In the east: Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to the vessel of the essence of taste (*rasa-tattva-pātra*).
Salutation to the vessel of the essence of form (*rūpa-tattva-pātra*) in the south. Salutation to the vessel of the essence of touch (*sparśa-tattva-pātra*) in the west.

Salutation to the vessel of the essence of sound (*śabda-tattva-pātra*) in the north. Having thus worshipped, one should place milk in the center, fruit in the east, honey in the south, and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) in the north.
Śakrāṅgula, having worshipped with the Brahma-mantras either sugarcane juice or coconut water in the north as before,
having consecrated it with the Brahma-aṅga [mantra], having invoked [the deity] and displayed the five mudrās, and having offered incense, lamps, and arghya,
one should place the substances in vessels in the four directions starting from the east.

Having mixed [the substances] into the middle vessel, consecrated it with the root mantra, and performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the protective encircling (*avakuṇṭhana*), one should consecrate the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) with the Vedic Brahmā-aṅga mantras. Following that, on the western side, having drawn a square measuring five *tāla*s upon a mound of three *droṇas* of rice grains and paddy, and having worshipped a lotus seat (*padmāsana*) upon it—

Having wrapped the nine jars and the *vardhanī* with thread, having washed them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having offered incense and a lamp with the *astra-mantra*, one should fill them with water and adorn them with fragrant substances,
gems, tufts of grass (*kūrca*), floating coconut shells, flower garlands, and so forth, as well as with scents, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and cloth, using the *astra-mantra*.

Having placed [the image] upon a lotus, one should worship it; having worshipped the form of Śiva’s seat in the center, one performs the rites of invocation, installation, and so forth, displays the five mudrās,
invokes Manonmani into the *vardhanī* vessel with her mantra, performs the installation and other rites, and [displays] the great mudrā of Padmayoni.

Having displayed [the deities] in the directions starting from the east, having worshipped them beginning with Ananteśa and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, having offered the food offering (naivedya), incense, lamp, and water for honor (arghya), and having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the sequence of the digits (kalā) such as Mātṛkā and so forth— this is the ritual bathing (snāpana). Now, the worship of the Sun (saurapūjā):

Now, regarding the worship of the Sun: one should worship the Sun either between Indra and Agni or in the northeast (Īśāna). Facing north in front of the Sun, having established the *arghya* offering with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and having sprinkled the door with the *astra-mantra*, [one worships] on the right and left sides of the door: "Salutation to Daṇḍin," "Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Piṅgala," "Salutation to Gaṇapati," and "Salutation to the Gurus. Having entered within, [one worships] on the seat: "Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Prabhūtāsana."
Homage!
(5th line) In the inner enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*), from the southwest (*naiṛtya*) to the northeast (*īśāna*): homage to Vimala, homage to Sāra, homage to Ārādhya, homage to Paramasukha.

(6th line) Homage to Padma—having thus displayed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*)—in the eight directions starting from the front of its face: *oṃ rāṃ dīptāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ rīṃ sūkṣmāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ* (7th line)...
Oṃ ruṃ, obeisance to Jayā; Oṃ rūṃ, obeisance to Bhadrā; Oṃ reṃ, obeisance to Vibhūti; Oṃ raiṃ, obeisance to Vimalā; Oṃ roṃ, obeisance to Amoghā.
Oṃ rauṃ, obeisance to Vidyutā; in the pericarp, in the northeast, Oṃ raḥ, obeisance to Sarvatomukhī. Having displayed the *visphura* mudrā, [one says]:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Arka; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Arka; Oṃ khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolka, the form of Sūrya;

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the two eyes of Bhānu; Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śiva-Sūrya together. Having invoked [the deity] with this mantra, one performs the installation and so forth with the five mudrās.
Having displayed [the mudrās] and offered incense, lamps, and water for honor (arghya), one should perform meditation.
"I bow to Āditya, the creator of all, endowed with fifteen digits (*kalā*), holding two lotuses in his hands, the sole witness of all the worlds. Having thus meditated,
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Gāyatrī, having worshipped the limbs, and having honored [the deity] with water from the vessel (*bimba-jala*).

Having worshipped the ten world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the third enclosure, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamp, and water for the guest (*arghya*), one should worship on the left with the mantra:

"Salutation to Tejaścaṇḍeśvara. Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the form (*mūrti*) using the root-mantra and the heart-mantra, and having performed the prostration—[thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of the Sun].
Now, the worship of Gaṇeśa:

Having sat with a serene face in the pavilion dedicated to Gaṇeśa, and having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other preliminary rites, the ritual identification (sakalīkaraṇa), and the sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa): "Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to the Lord of All," on the head; "Oṃ giṃ, salutation to the Destroyer of Obstacles," on the eyes.
Oṃ guṃ, salutation to Gajamukha at the waist; Oṃ gaiṃ, salutation to Ākhuvāhana at the thighs; Oṃ gauṃ, salutation to Vighneśvara at the knees;
Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśvara at the knees.

Thus, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the two feet with the five [mantras] beginning with *gaṇānāṃ tvā*, and having likewise performed the placement on the head, face, chest, private parts, knees, and feet with the five mantras beginning with *gaṇānāṃ tvā*, and having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), sprinkled [the deity] twice with the *āvaraṇa* mantras, and worshipped Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī above, one should worship Bhuvaṅga, Pataṅga, Kūśmāṇḍa, and Kumbhodara on the two sides with mantras ending in *namaḥ*. Then, by means of the root mantra, [one should place the deity] upon the jewel-throne (*maṇipīṭha*) in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*).

Having worshipped the "gām" seed-syllable and so forth, having well-worshipped the gatekeepers, and having worshipped Mahāsūra and Mūṣika in front, having performed the ritual service (*upacāra*), and having entered within— from the southwest to the northeast— one [should worship] Suta, Deva, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmīvijayā, [and the weapons] the noose, the goad, the triple-pronged trident, and the yoni. (F7a, line 1) Mahā-...
Having displayed the *namaskāra-mudrā* with the hands,
one should meditate upon the elephant-faced [deity] as having three eyes, the hue of saffron, and four arms.
And hold a noose and a tooth in your right hand, while in your left you hold a kusha-grass ring and a sweetmeat ball.
Having meditated thus, having consecrated [the deity] with the water for bathing such as unguents and other substances,
having adorned [him] with garments and so forth, and having worshipped as before, one should worship on the two sides with "Obeisance to Siddhalakṣmī and Vallabhā" in the second enclosure.
One should recite the eight forms of Gaṇeśa:
Yogaja,
Vighneśvara, Mahākhaṇḍa, Gajavaktra, and Mahodaka.
Having thus worshipped the single-tusked, great-bodied Vināyaka, the lord of the Gaṇas, in the third enclosure,
according to the *Cintya-tantra*:
The Child, the Devotee, the Bestower of all Success through Power,
Piṅgala, Ucchiṣṭa, Rakta, Kṣipra, and Heramba.
Lakṣmī, Vijayanṛtta, and likewise Ūrdhvāmaha (or Mahāgaṇa)—these sixteen yellow ones are to be known; one should worship them in the third [round].

In the fourth enclosure: at the foot of the Āgneya tree, salutation to Brahmā accompanied by Sarasvatī; in the southwest (Nairṛtya), at the foot of the Mandāra tree, salutation to Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī; in the northwest (Vāyavya), at the foot of the Kalpa tree, [salutation to] Bhavānī.

Salutation to Maheśvara united with [Umā] in the northeast at the foot of a sandalwood tree; salutation to Kāmadeva united with Rati. Having worshipped Indra and the other world-protectors in the fifth enclosure—

Having offered various foods such as coconuts and other grains, along with sacrificial offerings (*naivedya*) like sweetmeats (*modaka*) and rice-balls (*laḍḍuka*), incense, lamps, and water for the guest-offering (*arghya*);

and having distributed the *bali* offering to the door-keepers and other deities in the eight directions; and having worshipped at the *balipīṭha* with the mantra "Obeisance to the one who embodies the host of all obstacles" (*namaḥ sarvavighnagaṇarūpāya*); and having presented the *bali* with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the hosts of all obstacles" (*oṃ hāṃ sarvavighnagaṇebhyaḥ svāhā*); [one should offer] the obstructing *arghya* (*nirodhārghya*) in front.
Having cast [the offerings] and performed all the ritual services (*upacāra*), this concludes the worship of Vighneśvara. Now, for the worship of the Lord:
having approached the temple door and worshipped it on the right side with offerings such as coconut and so forth, one should [sprinkle] the door with *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*.

Having sprinkled [the site] and consecrated it, and having worshipped Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī in the south, north, and center respectively, one should worship [the deity] in the middle, on the right side [saying] "...namaḥ," on the left side [saying] "Gaṅgāyai namaḥ," and on the north side [saying] "Mahākālāya namaḥ" and "Yamunāyai namaḥ. Then, upon the two upper stones, [one worships] "Bhuvaṅgapataṅgābhyāṃ namaḥ."

On the right and left pillars: salutation to the two *utkāra* banners. On the two door-panels: salutation to Vimala; salutation to Subāhu. On the lintel (*paṭṭikā*): salutation to Skanda. On the two rings (*valaya*): salutation to Candra and Sūrya. Having worshipped the nine powers (*navaśakti*) in the cavity, [one offers] salutation to the Weapon (*astra*) in front, on the side of the southern wall.
(6th line) Homage to the weapon, the gatekeeper; homage to Daṇḍin.
And its mantra-eye has the form of reddish rays, with matted hair, a deer-face, and an upward gaze. (7th line)

Having meditated thus: "I worship the form of Dindi, who has placed his feet upward with his face turned up, whose pair of hands are blossomed, who smiles, holds a staff in his hand, and is adorned with a garland of victory-jewels," one should offer salutation to the right side [of the door] saying: "Obeisance to the Gatekeeper Astra; obeisance to Muṇḍin."
His body resembles a firebrand, his face is terrifying, and his matted hair stands erect.
He has a basket of laughter, and his hands display the *vāstu* mudrā.
He wears a noose bound around his waist, bracelets, and is adorned with snakes.
"I worship the form of Muṇḍī, who is served by sages, gods, and men.
Having thus meditated and offered the *arghya*, [one says]: "Salutation to Vṛṣabheśvara before me.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
His body is like silver, his feet are the Vedas, and his face is turned upward;
he has ruddy, upward-pointing horns, is the color of fire, and possesses three eyes.
He is adorned with a garland of *maṇi* gems and a string of small bells.

Having meditated thus upon the Primordial God, the Lord of the Bull, whose form is the Dharma of green hue, and having worshipped Him with the root mantra, one should invoke Him from whichever horn [of the bull] with the mantra "O Bull," perform the placement of the Gāyatrī, and offer the food offering (*naivedya*) to all. Then, having warded off the three kinds of obstacles—celestial, terrestrial, and those dwelling in the intermediate space—near the door, and having surveyed the celestial realm with divine vision... (7th line)

Having offered a flower with the mantra *huṃ phaṭ* while visualizing oneself as the deity and forming the appropriate mudrā, one should touch the ground three times with the big toe of the right foot while reciting the *astra-mantra*.

For the purpose of dispelling the three obstacles, one should strike the bell three times with the Astra-mantra on the northern side. Having entered within from the south, starting from the eastern foot, one worships the deities stationed at the gateway and those headed by Prakṛti upon the crown. At the time following the offering of the bali-oblation, having spread out the torn cloth with the Hṛdaya-mantra, [one recites] "Obeisance to Sthāṇu."
I worship Dhyānā, who is mounted upon a blue horse, adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments,
who covers the three worlds with her sleep, and who holds a bedstead as her weapon.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*). Having sprinkled the threshold of the inner sanctum with the *astra-mantra*, one should worship the enclosure of the womb (*garbhāvaraṇa*) starting from the southwest (*naiṛtya*) and ending at the northeast (*īśāna*). Having worshipped Brahmā, the lord of the site (*vāstvadhipati*), with the mantra "Brahmā as spoken by Nairṛta" and the formula "Obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site," one should worship Gaṇapati, who is seated in the west, with the *gaṇa-mantra*. Then, having worshipped Sarasvatī in the northwest with the mantra for the prostrated Sarasvatī—*praṇatasarasvatī-mantra*—[one should proceed].

In the north, having worshipped Lakṣmī with the mantra "hiraṇyavarṇām," and having worshipped the nine Śaktis beginning with Vāmā at the mouth of the cow with the mantra "devīm vācam," [one should worship] Sadāśiva and Ananta in the northeast with the mantra "sabrahmasaśiva," as well as Śrīkaṇṭha and Ambikā.

One should worship the seven gurus, according to the injunction: "One should worship the Guru, the Guha, Viṣṇu, and the Dhātṛ—the gurus in the seven [stages]. Thus, one should fully worship the seven gurus. Having taken hold of the consecration vessel with the Astra-mantra and filled it with water by means of the Mūla-mantra, one should invoke the nine holy fords (*navatīrtha*) into its midst with the Gaṅgā-mantra, "imaṃ me varuṇam. Then, having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, one should perform the Brahmāṅga-nyāsa twenty-one times and recite [the mantra] in this manner. With the Astra-mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
Having performed the ritual with the root mantra and having worshipped with the water for consecration, one should worship Rudra upon the top of the liṅga with the *yorūdreti* mantra. Then,
taking the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) with the thumb and forefinger, one should place it in the northeast direction with the heart-mantra, *namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ*.

Having established [the deity] with the *astra-mantra*, "samsthāpya pramuñcadhanvā," and having sprinkled the *liṅga* with the water of the *arghya* offering, one should place a single flower upon its head. Then, having washed the *liṅga* with the *pāśupatāstra-mantra*, "oṃ śrīṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ," and having [cleansed] both the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* using a *kūrca* brush...

"Having purified" refers to the purification of the *liṅga*. Having visualized the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) in the *mūlādhāra*, having applied a forehead mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead with the heart-mantra and the secret mantra, and having placed a flower on the crest-lock (*śikhā*) with the root-mantra, one should recite the *ambhaka* [mantra] from the beginning to the end of the *nāda* within the *suṣumṇā*, extending from the base to the top of the head, in order to remove impurity from the mantras.

Reciting the Śiva-mantra ten times, one should consecrate each limb with the Brahmāṅga-mantras; this is the purification of the mantra (*mantra-śuddhi*). Because of the movement of the teeth, palate, and lips, there may be defects in the limbs indicated by the mantra-soul; to avoid those defects, the utterance of the *nādānta* (the final sound) is prescribed. Next, regarding the worship of the five seats (*pañcāsana*), [it begins] upon the foundation stone (*ādhāra-śilā*).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti.
She is seated upon the tortoise-stone below, her body white as the ocean of milk;
she has the form of a seed-sprout upon her crown and bestows boons and fearlessness. (3rd line)
Having meditated thus upon the Śakti Kriyā, who holds a noose and a goad and whose form is the foundation,
one should then meditate upon that which is above her.

Having meditated thus upon the *Ādhāraśakti*— who is white as a jasmine flower or a conch shell, who bestows boons, who has three eyes, who possesses necklaces and armlets numbering ten million, who grants fearlessness, and who holds a noose and a goad in her right and left hands, with the sun and moon as her crest-ornaments— one should [place] Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and Kārkoṭaka in the four directions starting from the east upon the *brahmaśilā*.
Having performed worship from the southeast to the northeast, one worships Śaṅkhapāla, Gulika, Padma, and Mahāpadma. Then, in the northeast, [one recites]:

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Anantāsana. Thus, having visualized the seat of Ananta and the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*) extending from the front plank of the pedestal up to the neck, [one proceeds] from the southeast to the northeast.

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Dharma," "Salutation to Jñāna," "Salutation to Vairāgya," and "Salutation to Aiśvarya," one should discard [the opposite qualities] starting from the east and ending in the north: "Salutation to Adharma," "Salutation to Ajñāna," "Salutation to Avairāgya," and "Salutation to Anaiśvarya. [One should worship] above the throat, on the right, left, and in the middle.

Having worshipped the *rājasa*, *tāmasa*, and *sāttvika* [qualities], one should again worship the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas in the four directions starting from the southeast (Āgneyī). In the center, [one should worship] the Yogāsana with "Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the Lion Throne" (*simhāsanāya namaḥ*), extending from the upper neck upwards to the upper band.

Between Īśāna and Pūrva, [one should worship] "Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the Unmanifest" (*avyaktāya namaḥ*). Between Dakṣiṇa and Agni, [one should worship] "Salutation to Niyati" (*niyatiṣṭhāya namaḥ*). Between Nairṛti and Varuṇa... [F11b, line 1]

In the middle [of the line], the *kalā* [...]. Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Keśava between Vāyu and Soma," one should worship them with "Obeisance to Sandalwood in the northeast" on the second line below.

"Salutation to Ūrdhvachadana; salutation to Yogāsana in Īśāna. Thus, having visualized the Yogāsana as a blooming white lotus seat upon the upper plank, [one should visualize] from the base of the plank at the region of the *ādhāra* (foundation), starting from the east and ending in the northeast.

Having worshipped [the lotus] from its bulb, seed, sprout, stalk, thorns, petals, filaments, and pericarp, extending outwards in the eight directions, one should worship the lotus seat in the center with: *oṃ hāṃ padmāsanāya namaḥ*. Then, on the eight petals in the eight directions, one should worship:
*oṃ hāṃ vāmāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ raudryai namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ kālyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ*... [6th line].
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kalavikaraṇī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Balavikaraṇī;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Balapramathinī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Manonmanī. Having displayed the *namaskāra-mudrā* upon the pericarp, one should contemplate three circles within the filaments at the edge of the band, ending with the root mantra in the center. On the right side of the outermost circle, [one should offer]: "Salutation to Ātmatattva; salutation to Brahmā, the lord of Ātmatattva. On the north [side]...
Homage to the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*); homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge.
In the center, homage to the principle of Śiva (*śiva-tattva*); homage to Rudra, the lord of the principle of Śiva.

(4th line) Having visualized the pericarp in the middle of the circle’s perimeter, and having contemplated three mandalas within it, [one offers] "homage to the solar mandala" in the first mandala. (5th line)

Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar orb; salutation to the lunar orb in the second circle; salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar orb. (Sixth line) Salutation to the fiery orb in the third circle; salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fiery orb.
Upon the *liṅga* situated within the maṇḍala, above the portion of Rudra (*rudrabhāga*),
and above the base (*mūla*), one should invoke the Sadāśiva-maṇḍala [beginning with] *ā*...; the visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows:

Having meditated thus: "The pair of arms [of the deity] holds a lotus at the left eye of the Goddess and a water-pot at the tip of the feet of Gomukha; the *liṅga* is firmly established upon the pedestal in the middle of the *yoni*, its nature being that of Sadāśiva and Manonmanī placed therein"—one should offer salutation with: *oṃ hāṃ sadāśivamaṇḍalāya namaḥ sadāśivamaṇḍalādhipataye*.
(3rd line) Salutation to Sadāśiva.
The meditation (*dhyāna*):
O Mother, whose divine form is the Great One, the Self, and the Sky, together with [the letters]... may you [be present].

Thus, having worshipped Śakti with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śakti," within the Bīja which reveals all mantras, I, though great, bow even once to you, O Sundarī, the supreme Manī, the Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā), who are present in the retinue. Then, having divided the worship of the Cause into three parts, one should worship the portion belonging to Rudra— the Lord of the central region— as the vessel.

At the upper portion, one should worship Sadāśiva, Vahni, Soma, Ravi, Śakti, and the blissful seat of Śiva-Śakti. Above the Rudra-portion, one should divide the mandala into five parts; having performed the worship of the five [deities], one should perform the extraction (*udhāraṇa*). At the beginning of this, in the Viṣṇu-portion, one should worship the Lotus Yoga-seat (*padmayogāsana*); then, in the Siṃha-seat... (line 2).

One should worship [the deities] in the Brahma-portions; having worshipped Īśvara in the front portion, one should always worship Sadāśiva. Without the limbs such as the staff-bending and so forth, one should perform the Muṇḍa [rite]. Thus, having worshipped in this sequence—

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śakti-maṇḍala; obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Vimalāsana. Thus [are the] five seats. Above that, in the portion of Sadāśiva, [one says]: obeisance to the Sadāśivāsana. Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva; Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the body of knowledge; Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the eyes; Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva," and having fully worshipped the five Brahmās beginning with Īśāna in the order starting from Īśāna, one worships [the deity] in the causal [state] for the purpose of invocation and for the purpose of enjoyment.

Having placed a single flower with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) in the left hand and performed the five purifications (*pañca-śuddhi*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Īśāna and the others, ending with Sadyojāta, using the seed-syllables of the five Brahmās starting from the thumb; then,

having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa*) starting from the little finger and ending with the thumb using the long vowels as seed-syllables, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the protection of the site (*rakṣaṇa*) with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*).

Having formed the añjalīmudrā and meditated upon Sadāśiva, there shall be the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) in the place of the yogi for the invocation and seating; through worship, there shall be the great lotus (mahāpadma).

The hymn for the one named Vimalabhojin is recited during dance and song, and he is said to be seated upon an infinite throne (*anantāsana*). Having meditated [upon him] as having five faces like the moon and ten arms,

holding a trident, an axe, a sword, and a thunderbolt in the right hands, and a noose, a parasol, a goad, a jewel, and fire in the left hands, and possessing the nature of Śiva seated upon a white lotus— having thus meditated...

The procedure for the invocation of Kāmika, Svayambhu, and Devikā—[the sequence of the rite of invocation], as well as the [use of] the thumbs and the lingas—is recorded as the method of invocation. Regarding the invocation for other lingas: with one's own heart-mantra, [one should place] the seat of Śiva and the form of Śiva between the throat and the eyes, above the head, in the location of the *dvādaśānta*.

Having meditated upon the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva with a gracious mind, having unified them through *recaka* (exhalation), and having joined them with Sadāśiva upon the placed flower through *kumbhaka* (retention), one should meditate on the flower as radiant as ten million moons. Then, performing the installation with the mantra "namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ," one should bring the heart-seat (*hṛdayāsana*) to the palms joined in *añjali*, contemplate it in the form of a drop (*bindu*), mount it upon the tip of the cloth, and gaze there with divine vision through *recaka*.
Having invoked [the deity] from the heart of the Vasus with the *udbhava-mudrā* and the root mantra ending in *namaḥ* above the top of the *liṅga*, having established [it] with the right hand,

having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Brahma-limbs in sequence by means of the "staff-bending" (*daṇḍabhaṅgi*) gesture, having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the rite of immortality (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), and having offered the *arghya* with the root mantra of the five faces and six limbs— (F14b, line 1)

Having sequentially deposited the five Brahmans in the manner of a broken staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*) starting from *Sthiti* and ending at the region of Rudra, one should deposit the Śivāsana and the form of Śiva (*śivamūrti*) in the place of Maheśvara;

having deposited the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), one should deposit the three eyes in the portion of Śivā; then, having deposited the five Īśānas starting from the head and ending at the portion of Rudra, one should again [deposit] the Śivāsana.

Having performed the sixteen-limbed rite, having performed the placement [of mantras], having bound the directions, and having rendered [the elements] nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛtya*), one should place the *mātrikās* in the form of *kalās* in their proper order; then, having placed Ananta in the left hand and a flower, and having performed the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*) and so forth as before, one should form the *añjali* mudrā with the mantra: *nassarvavidyānām*.

Having invoked [the deity] with the mantra beginning with *sadyojātam* and ending with *pra...* [and so forth], and having performed the rites from installation (*sthāpana*) up to the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) using the *hṛdaya-mantra* and the primary weapon-mantras (*astramantra*). Then, the installation (*sthāpana*) is performed with the mantra *namo vaḥ kirikebhyo...*; the presence (*sannidhāna*) is indicated by the words *asmin haste na vedi*; and the confinement (*nirodhana*) is performed with the mantra *yā te rudra...* [and so forth]. Adhyavo... [F15a, line 1].

Having thus performed the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) with the mantra *tryambakaṃ yajāmahe*, the supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*), and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the mantra *pramuñca dhanvanas*, and having offered the water of honor (*arghya*),

one should offer three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while reciting the Śiva-Gāyatrī mantra. Having displayed the five mudrās beginning with Īśāna upon the five faces, and having displayed the great five-faced *añjali* mudrā in the center with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [one should proceed].
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Śiva—this is the water for sipping (ācamana). Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Śiva—thus [offering] the arghya;

having given the water for the feet, the arghya, the water for sipping, and so forth, as well as incense and the lamp, one should recite the Rudrasūkta and other mantras of the Padas once. This is the invocation... Having worshipped the lion-throne for the purpose of the consecration (abhiṣeka), one should place a flower upon the top of the liṅga with the root mantra ending in vauṣaṭ, [and then worship] the God.
One should pray: "O God of gods, Lord of the World, whose nature is five-faced; for the sake of the consecration for the protection of the day, turn toward me who am facing upward.
Having prayed thus, one should take the vessel of consecration with the root mantra and [visualize] the Moon, Sun, and Fire in the middle of the lip on the back of the vessel.

Having worshipped the maṇḍala and having worshipped with the root mantra, one should perform the consecration upon observing the time of the moon and sun. In the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*, it is stated: "Worship at the time when the moon and sun [are eclipsed] bestows all accomplishments; worship at a time devoid of that [lunar-solar conjunction] shall be fruitless. The sun is situated at the upper limit, while the moon is the vital breath below. Having brought about the restraint of these two, it is known as being "devoid of the lunar form" (*candrakāra-hita*).

In this manner, having sequentially restrained the upward and downward vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*), one should take water filled from the flask according to the number [of recitations] of the *Mūlamantra* and *Kālottara*, mixed with fragrance, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*); then, drawing it up by exhalation (*recaka*) and holding it with retention (*kumbhaka*) above the lotus and other [parts],
one should bind it with both the left and right hands and consecrate the top of the *liṅga* with a stream four finger-breadths wide, the measure of a cow’s horn.

Again, having consecrated the oil with the *hṛdaya* [mantra], and having smeared the *liṅga* and its pedestal with powdered *āmalaka* using the *kavaca* [mantra], having sprinkled them with pure water and empowered them with the *vyomavyāpin* [mantra], one should offer incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering; then, with the *astra* [mantra], [one prepares] milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugarcane, and *bilva* fruit with the *astra* [mantra].

Having consecrated the *arghyodaka* with the mantra of the worlds (*bhuvana*), the digits (*kalā*), and the principles (*tattva*), and having consecrated the water mixed with turmeric upon the pedestal (*piṭha*) with the *śānti* mantra,

one should consecrate it with scented water using the root mantra (*mūla*). Then, as the special *arghyodaka*, one should use scented water mixed with musk, camphor, saffron, and lotus paste, [consecrated] with the root mantra.
Having smeared the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) with [fragrant substances], having worshipped with flowers using the *hṛdaya-mantra*,

and having offered food offerings (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*), one should sprinkle them with water. Then, by means of the root mantra, one performs the thousand-stream consecration (*sahasradhārābhiṣeka*), followed by the bathing water from the nine jars (*navakalaśasnapanodaka*), the water from the conch (*śaṅkhodaka*), and the pure water (*śuddhodaka*) purified by the five Brahmās.
Having consecrated [the image], having placed a single flower upon its head,

[one should perform] the anointing and so forth with ground *āmalaka* and other substances, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), clay from a cremation ground, milk, curd, ghee, honey, *lakṣū* fruit, coconut, fragrant water for bathing, and a conch shell.
Having performed a dance with a washed cloth and having applied an ointment upon the *viratantra*, one should not perform purification with that same washed cloth;

rather, having displayed it before the sun with an upper garment, [one should adorn oneself] with perfumes suitable for the occasion, flower garlands, sacred threads, along with silk headbands, earrings, necklaces, strings of pearls, and so forth.

Having performed the ritual adornment of the *liṅga-deha* according to the rules, one should provide yellow cloth for the *kāraṇa-liṅga* in the forenoon; red cloth at midday; and [white] cloth during the half-watch [of the afternoon]. In the absence of these, one should have cloth made that is suitable for all times. Furthermore, according to the measurement for the *libhotsava*, there should be: first, wrapping with cloth; second, ornaments; third, beautified with flowers; and fourth...
One should smear all the limbs with fragrant ointment;

having offered a flower with the root mantra and displayed the *namaskāra* mudrā, the wise one should likewise place the *liṅga-pīṭha* in the center and the five *pratyāṅgas*. One should worship Īśāna on the head, and Īśa in the east.

One should worship Aghora in the eastern face, Vāmadeva in the northern face, and Sadyojāta in the western face. Having worshipped the [mantra] ending in *gika* in the southeast, one should worship the Heart in the north; having worshipped the Śikhā in the northwest, one should worship the Armor in the northeast. One should place the Eye in the center, and at the top of the directions, those ending with the word "namas."

With the mantras "Hṛdayāya Svāhā," "Vaiṣaṭ," "Hṛt," "Tathā Vauṣaṭ," and ending with "Auh Phat," one should worship above the head. Having thus worshipped the first [layer], one should worship the second upon the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*). In the middle of the petals of the *vidyārāja*, one should worship according to the upper row. One should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others; this constitutes the threefold enclosure. Then, according to the lower row, one should worship the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*) in the fourfold enclosure, as well as their weapons.

One should worship [the deity] upon the stone... thus is the configuration of the faces described, as well as the configuration of the bodies. One should worship Sadāśiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Vidhīśvara, starting from the eastern face and ending with Īśāna. The five faces consist of the five beginning with Īśāna.
One should worship the twenty-five bodies of the five deities, O Lord of Gods. Likewise, the downward-facing one is situated below; in this sequence, the head is in the region of Īśāna.
Oṃ Hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna in the east; obeisance to Tatpuruṣa-vaktra in the south; obeisance to Aghora-hṛdaya in the north;
obeisance to Vāmadeva-guhya in the west; obeisance to Sadyojāta-mūrti in the rear—having thus worshipped [them], [one worships] Amśumatī, Gaurī, Gaṅgā, and Nārtha.

The five powers are Ambikā and the others. Thus, one should worship the five powers in the directions beginning with Īśāna: "Salutation to the Heart" in the southeast; "Svāhā, salutation to the Head" in the southwest; "Vauṣaṭ to the Crest" in the northwest; "Huṃ to the Armor" in the northeast; "Vaiṣaṭ to the Three Eyes" in the center; and "Hastrayahuphaṭ" in the northeast of that [center]. Having thus worshipped, one should say: "Salutation to the Body of Knowledge" in the portion belonging to Maheśvara.

In the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*), one should worship the seven Śaktis: Sūkṣmā in the northeast; Abhimāninī in the region of Nirṛti; Śakti in the southeast; Pāśā in the southwest; Aṅkuśā at the head of Khaṭvāṅginī; Gaṅgā in the region of Īśa; and Vidyā in the northwest. One should worship these seven Śaktis.
On the upper band of the pedestal, in the eight petals starting from the east and proceeding clockwise:
*oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ sūkṣmāya namaḥ*,
*oṃ hāṃ śivottamāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ ekanetrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ ekarudrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ trimūrtaye namaḥ*.
Having worshipped thus with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin," and having fully honored the eight Vidyeśvaras, one should worship the Śaktis:
"Dhṛti, Svadhā, Kṣamā, Puṣṭi, Kīrti, and Medhā—this is the auspicious group of eight named Śaktis. (F19a, line 1)
Having performed worship, one should worship with a pair [of mantras] in each of the four directions beginning from the ear and the body; in the third enclosure, between Indra and Īśāna:
*oṃ hāṃ nandine namaḥ*; between Indra and Agni: *oṃ hāṃ mahākālāya namaḥ*; between Yama and Agni: *oṃ hāṃ bhṛṅgiṇe*.
Salutation between Yama and Nairṛti: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Between Nairṛti and Varuṇa: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabha.
(4th line) Between Vāyu and Varuṇa: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Skanda. Between Vāyu and Kubera: Salutation to the Goddess.
(5th line) Between Īśāna and... [text ends]

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Caṇḍa in the middle of Kubera and Yama," one should worship the Śaktis: Kaṇṭhī, Kālakaṇṭhī, Mohinī, Mālinī, Nandinī, Vanāvallī, Mati, and Bhūtā—these are the eight Śaktis. Having thus worshipped in the fourth enclosure, then on the eastern plank: Oṃ Hāṃ Laṃ... (F19b, line 1).
*Indrāya namaḥ*. *Raṃ agnaye namaḥ*. *Yaṃ yamāya namaḥ*. *Kṣaṃ nirṛtyai namaḥ*. *Saṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*. *Vaṃ vāyave namaḥ*.
*Haṃ kuberāya*. (Second line)

"Salutation to Śam Īśāna; salutation to the south of Īśāna: Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. To the north-west of Nairṛti: Oṃ (third line) Hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Having worshipped thus, one should worship the Śaktis: "Śacī, Svāhā, Kālakarṇī, Jātā, Cāhu, Hariṇī, Añjanā, Dagdhā, Jīvā, and the goddess Varadā—these are the Śaktis of the directions. Having worshipped thus, in the fifth enclosure, on the Ādhāra-śakti, in the cardinal and intermediate directions beginning with the east... (fifth line).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vajra; homage to Śakti; homage to Daṇḍa; homage to Khaṭvāṅga;

homage to Pāśa; homage to Aṅkura; homage to Gadā; (sixth line) homage to Triśūla; homage to Cakra; homage to Padma. Having worshipped [these], one should worship Śakti, who is indeed Vilāsūrūpiṇī, Dhāriṇī, and Vimukhī.
(First line) Likewise, [worship] Nirmali and Durmali-devī, Matiśrī, and Samā; [then] the swan-necked one who bestows peace, and the powers of the weapons.
(Second line) Having thus worshipped these in the fivefold enclosure of the causal [deity], first [worship] Brahmā and the others in front, then the Vidyeśvaras and the Gaṇeśvaras. (Third line)

And [the worship] of the guardians of the directions (*dikpālakas*), the ten weapons, and the Lord (*īśa*) according to the sequence of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*). Then, below the *brahmapaṭikā*: first, to the east, "Oṃ, obeisance to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*);

obeisance to the principle of the ego (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of touch (*tvak-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of sight (*cakṣus-tattva*). (Line 6)
Homage to the principle of the tongue; homage to the principle of breath; homage to the principle of the feet; homage to the principle of the hands; homage to the principle of the anus;

homage to the principle of the generative organ; homage to the principle of touch; homage to the principle of form; homage to the principle of taste; homage to the principle of smell; homage to the principle of space.
Having worshipped with "Oṃ namo vāyutattvāya, namo agnitattvāya, namaḥ kālatattvāya, namaḥ pṛthivitattvāya," [one should then recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ namo ātmatattvāya;
namo brahmaṇe, the lord of the principle of the self (ātmatattva), whose form is emanation (sṛṣṭirūpa), accompanied by Sarasvatī. [Then recite] "brahmajajñānam... (Rig Veda 10.72.6).
Having worshipped with this mantra,
according to the *Siddhāntaratnākara*,
the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
And [he saw] Brahmā, four-faced, four-armed, with matted hair rising upward,
endowed with a rosary and staff, bestowing boons and fearlessness, and auspicious.

Having meditated thus and worshipped the Gāyatrī, one should worship from the root-lord (*kandeśa*) up to the upper fillet (*ūrdhvapaṭṭikā*), and from the lower part of the upper fillet down to the edge on the side of Viṣṇu, according to the previously mentioned procedure: "Oṃ, obeisance to the principle of Māyā (*māyā-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of Puruṣa (*puruṣa-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of Rāga (*rāga-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of Vidyā (*vidyā-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of Kalā (*kalā-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of Niyati (*niyati-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of Kalā (*kalā-tattva*). Having worshipped thus, [one recites] "Oṃ."
Hrīṃ, homage to the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva).

Homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge, who possesses the form of the presiding Rudra (sthitirudra), accompanied by Lakṣmī; having worshipped him with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ... [and so forth].

I bow to the peaceful Paravāsudeva, who is in the state of meditative absorption, whose form is known as blue, whose lotus-face is [radiant], who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who bears the discus as his weapon, and whose crown is adorned with a conch.

Having meditated thus and performed the *nyāsa* of the *gāyatrī*, one should proceed from east to west, encircling the area from the upper band (*ūrdhvapaṭṭikā*) up to the portion belonging to Rudra, [reciting]: "Salutation to the Śiva-tattva; salutation to the Lord of Śiva-nature; salutation to him whose form is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*);
salutation to Rudra together with Rudrāṇī," while consecrating [the area] with the mantra "yo rudro... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.1).

I bow to the form of Rudra, who is established upon a deer; he possesses nine eyes enriched with meditation, wears a serpent as a sacred thread, and has two hands with palms joined. His throat is dark blue like fire, and in his left [hands] he holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, a trident, a rosary, and fire.
Having meditated thus and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *gāyatrī*, this is the worship of the three triads of principles (*tritattva*).

(3rd line) Now, in the upper portion of Maheśvara, one should worship the "City of Eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*): *namaḥ* to the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of taste (*rasa-tattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of form (*rūpa-tattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of touch (*sparśa-tattva*), and *namaḥ* to the principle of sound (*śabda-tattva*).
(5th line) Having worshipped with "namaḥ," [one offers salutation] to Maheśvara, who is of the nature of concealment and accompanied by Maheśvarī;
he who is proclaimed as the primordial sound at the beginning of the Vedas. (6th line)
And having consecrated [it] with the mantra "established in Vedānta," the meditation is as follows:
four-faced, eight-armed, and endowed with twelve eyes.
Holding a skeleton drum, a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup,
endowed with hands in the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness,
adorned with a sacred thread, red in hue, wearing sandals upon his feet, and decorated with a crown of matted locks.

Having meditated thus and consecrated the Gāyatrī, one should worship the portion of Sadāśiva with the following: "Salutation to the gross principle (*sthūlatattva*); salutation to the subtle principle (*sūkṣmatattva*); salutation to the time-principle (*kālatattva*).
Then, with the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," one should worship Sadāśiva, who is of the nature of grace and accompanied by Manonmanī.
Having consecrated it with mantras, one should meditate on [the deity] whose form resembles the autumnal moon and who is endowed with five faces.
Endowed with ten arms, with a tiger skin [draped] in this very manner,
standing on two feet, wearing variegated garments and so forth, adorned with all ornaments,
joined with a crown of matted hair, and equipped with an axe and a trident.
She holds the vajra joined with the "existence" mudrā and the gesture of fearlessness in her right hands;
she should likewise hold the noose, the boon-granting gesture, the bell, fire, and the goad.
"O gods, [one should meditate] upon that which is held in the left hand, having the form of light in its center.

Having thus meditated and performed the *nyāsa* of the *Gāyatrī*, one should worship Maheśa—the reality (*tattva*) consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) and its qualities—along with his retinue (*rāśika*), using the mantra; this is auspicious and brings about all accomplishments. Thus, on the seat of Śiva, which is the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*).

Having worshipped the form, having worshipped it with the limbs of Brahmā—the three eyes of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) and so forth—and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the parts of the *mātṛkā* and other kalās; then, having displayed the five mudrās beginning with the *dhenu*, and having offered incense and lamps, one should provide water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Then, having performed the "breaking of the staff" (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*) as the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) for Vijayā, and the "breaking of the head" (*muṇḍabhaṅgika*) as the limb of the root-mantra (*mūlāṅga*), one should worship.

In the same manner, having worshipped the entire sequence of offerings, as well as the food offering (*naivedya*), the water for honor (*arghya*), and the pure seat (*vimalāsana*), one should place the vessel of oblation upon a three-legged stand with the left knee [resting on the ground]. Then, having struck the bell with the *astra* mantra—
[this is] the cause.
Asuras, rākṣasas, piśācas,
and brahmarākṣasas likewise proceed by means of the sound of the word "maṇi" as their messenger.

Having offered oblations and betel at the door of Vighneśvara, and subsequently, having worshipped the offering-stand in the presence of the deity with the Astra-mantra, performed the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*), placed a flower in the center of the oblation, displayed the great mudrās such as the *dhenu* and others, rendered it nectar-like with the Kavaca-mantra, and sprinkled it while reciting *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*.

Having sprinkled [water] around the food and prepared it, one should recite the *Annasūkta* with the mantra "To Prāṇa, Svāhā. Having offered [the food] by circling it clockwise with one's own hand, and having contemplated that it has been given by the hand of Gaurī, one should join the food with the *Śivahasta* mudrā and unite it with the *Prakṛti-hasta*. Then, having given the *uttarāpośana* water with the *Sūktāṃte* mantra, one should set aside the cooking vessel in another place and [use] pure water for the purpose of washing the hands and feet.
Having offered [the oblation] three times:
according to the Kāmika, pure rice is for the upward-facing [mouth], while rice with jaggery is for the eastern-facing [mouth].
One should offer sesame-rice to the southern face, and likewise mung-bean rice to the northern;
one should present the five-faced [deity] with offerings ending in milk-pudding (*pāyasa*) to the western face.
[These include] the fruit of the wood-apple (*kapittha*), its core, and even that which is eaten by elephants.
One should act in such a way that the consumed [substances] are presented as the emblem and the face;

having offered the vessel for the ritual sipping (ācamana) and the vessel for the respectful offering (arghya) with one or five counts, and having placed them above the hands and upon the feet, one should show the facial cleansing powder and mouth-perfume together with cardamom, cloves, and camphor pellets.

Having offered betel leaf and performed the half-portion of ritual services (*upacāra*), having fully worshipped the infinite seat (*anantāsana*), and having displayed the five faces along with their limbs through the sequence of measures (*mātrākrama*) by means of incense,

lamps, and so forth, one should pray and dismiss [the deity]. Then, having washed the hands, one performs the *nīrājana* ceremony with the *ārātrika* and other items, followed by sacred ash (*bhasma*), the mirror (*darpaṇa*), the umbrella (*chatra*), the fly-whisk (*cāmara*), the fan (*vyajana*), and betel leaf (*tāmbūla*).

Having performed the ritual service in due order by offering the *prastārya* vessel, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), mantras, flowers, and benedictions (*āśīrvāda*), one should thereafter cause the recitation [of the scriptures] in the sequence of the four Vedas,
the *adhyayana-sūtras*, the *Purāṇas*, Dravidian hymns, and the *Gītās*. Then, in the dance pavilion, [one should perform] with rhythmic clapping (*tāla*) and percussion instruments (*maddala*).

One should offer services such as song and dance; this is the procedure for Śivā. Following the worship with the powers of enjoyment (*bhogaśakti*), then, in the northern part of the main hall, one should perform the rite of the seat, the form, and so forth, using the mantra of Umā.

Having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra and displayed the five mudrās beginning with the *sthāpana*, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the twenty-five *kalās* of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*), and having sprinkled the Śakti with the water of the *arghya* for the sake of consecration using the root mantra, one should first remove her garment, perform an anointing (*udvartana*) with a cloth, and adorn her with garments, perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
Having adorned [the seat] with golden ornaments, light, and so forth, and having worshipped the lotus seat, one should invoke Gāyatrī and consecrate it over the heart-center ten times;
[this is] the meditation. (5th line)
Dark-complexioned, wearing variegated garments, with a lotus-like face, her body adorned with peaceful ornaments;
her hair tied up, in the three-fold bend (*tribhaṅgī*) posture, bent by the weight of her breasts, with long legs and downcast face;
possessing the limbs of yoga and the power of enjoyment, with her left lotus-hand holding a white water-lily.
"O Goddess, eternally gracious, with eyes of supreme victory, Goddess of the gods, salutations to you.

(7th line) Having thus meditated, and having worshipped [the deity] together with the Śakti using the Brahmā-aṅgas beginning with Īśāna, one should worship [the deities] from Vāmā to Sarvabhūtadamana in the eight directions starting from the east in the second enclosure.
(F24b, 1st line)

Having worshipped Maheśvarī in the center, having fully worshipped the Śaktis of Indra and the others in the eight directions beginning with the east, and having worshipped Sarasvatī to the south-east and Mahālakṣmī to the north-west, one should offer the food offering, incense, lamps, and water for honor; [this is the procedure for the worship of the Power of Enjoyment]. The fire-rite: (-)
In the northeast,

having prepared either a square or circular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit, provided with three ridges (*mekhalā*) and elevated according to the prescribed rite, in the sacrificial pavilion or the kitchen; and having fashioned the navel above the upper ridge, sitting facing east or north upon the region of the navel, and having performed the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other rites to effect the ritual identification (*sakalīkṛtya*).

With the *pavitra* in hand, having prepared the common *arghya* with the *praṇava*, he sprinkles the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *arghya* water; having smeared that site with cow dung while reciting the *astra-mantra*, he performs the purification (*mārjana*).
Having placed the ritual materials to his right and performed the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*), he adorns the pit with the five powders (*pañcacūrṇa*) according to the rule.

Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), having worshipped the five *kalās* in the east, south, west, north, and center, having encircled [the site] with a three-stranded thread while reciting the *astra-mantra*,

and having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Ananta, and the others, one should draw the lines with one's hand holding *darbha* grass while reciting the *ullekhana-mantras*. Having worshipped the four-legged [altar] in the center with the *astra-mantra*, [one should worship] in the middle, north, and south.

(3rd line) Having worshipped the gods beginning with Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, and having worshipped Raudrī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī upon another line, one should place four footprints (catuṣpadāni) in their midst.

(4th line) Having laid down kusha grass with its tips pointing east and north using the Astra-mantra, and having established a protective door with darbha grass using the Kavaca-mantra, [one should act] in the middle region. (5th line)
Having worshipped Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara upon the two *kūrca* seats with perfumes and other offerings, and having placed the fire from the kitchen in either an earthen or a copper vessel,

one should take that fire and deposit it on the left side of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), worship it with the root mantra, and then [invoke] the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) into the center of the fire by way of the *suṣumnā* channel.

Having cast that [substance] together with the fire-seeds (*agnibīja*) by means of *kumbhaka*, and having made the *bindu*-fire radiant by means of *recaka*, one should join the fire, worship it, and visualize it as the Śiva-fire; then,

having worshipped it with the root mantra, one should place the fire-vessel in the southeast or the northeast, and [dispose of] the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) in the southwest on a fragment of firewood.

Having drawn [the fire] out and placed it in the center of the fire-pit, having worshipped it together with the three principles (*tattva*) and so forth, having invoked it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and contemplated it as being of the nature of consciousness, one should place it in the fire-vessel above the navel; then, within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), upon the *kūrca* grass, one should visualize Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara in their youthful forms.
In meditation,
I contemplate the Mother of the Supreme Fire— possessing a dark form, endowed with beautiful youth, her hair adorned with a garland of moons, her face like the full moon, and overflowing with nectar.

Having meditated thus, [one should worship] with "Āṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Having worshipped her in this manner, one should worship Vāgīśvara in her vicinity. The meditation is as follows: [He is] three-eyed, five-faced, white in color, and four-armed.
The all-pervading Lord of Speech, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a rosary and a lotus.

Having meditated thus, one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ*. Then, having veiled the fire with the *saṃhitā-mantra* and having circled it, one should—while standing with knees on the ground and hands raised—with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), lift the fire along with its tip using both hands and unite it with the vessel via the path of the *yoni*. Having placed the vessel in the region of the navel of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should proceed].

Having sprinkled it with water and scattered flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having set it aside in another place for the sake of purification after the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) following impurity, one should sprinkle a drop of water with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
cover it with fuel sticks while reciting the *varma-mantra*, kindle it with the *astra-mantra*, and worship the embryonic fire (*garbhāgni*) with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) ending in *namaḥ*.

Having consecrated [the darbha ring] with the Astra-mantra for the protection of the fetus, having tied the darbha bracelet upon the hand of the lady with the Kavaca-mantra, having worshipped it with the Sadyojāta-mantra for the purpose of securing the conception, and having offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the Hṛdaya-mantra; then, in the third month, for the sake of the *pumsavana* rite, having worshipped with the Vāmadeva-mantra and offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the Śiras-mantra, he should sprinkle three drops of water. In the sixth month, for the sake of the *sīmantonnayana* rite...
Having worshipped with the Aghora mantra and offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the Śikhā-mantra,

one should again consecrate [the image] three times with that same mantra for the purpose of fashioning the faces and limbs; then, in the tenth month, having fully worshipped with the Tatpuruṣa mantra for the sake of birth, one offers oblations of sesame seeds.

Having offered the three [syllables] with the *kavaca* mantra, one should consecrate them three times with its own mantra for the purpose of arranging the faces and limbs; having worshipped them for the purpose of "birth," one should contemplate the fire as being born.
For the purpose of the postnatal purification bath (*garbhāśauca-snāna*), one should sprinkle the fire with *darbha* grass and other materials, beginning with the bracelet on the hand of the Goddess.

Having cleansed [the child] with the *mūla-mantra*, and having tied a golden bracelet on the left hand of the Goddess for the protection of the child, one should worship [her] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Then, for the purpose of releasing the impurity (*sūtaka*), one should worship the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *astra-mantra*, sprinkle it [with water], strike it with *darbha* grass, and sprinkle it again with the *varma-mantra*. For the protection of the fire, [one should place] seven *darbhas* starting from the east within the middle girdle (*mekhalā*).

Having laid down the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa) and established the enclosing sticks (paridhi) in the four directions with the Astra-mantra, one should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) for the purpose of removing the saliva from the fires.

Having sprinkled clarified butter (ājya) on both the roots and tips [of the sticks], and having offered them with the fire-mantra (agnimantra) and the exclamation "svāhā," [one should proceed] in the four directions starting from the east, at the locations of the enclosing sticks.
Having worshipped the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Ananta in the east, and having placed two fuel-sticks— one upright and one horizontal— for protection with the Aghora weapon-mantra,

one should worship the *viṣṭara* in the east with "Obeisance to Indra," and then worship in sequence through the eight directions ending with Īśāna. Having worshipped Brahmā and Viṣṇu as previously described, [one should worship] the fire...

Having sprinkled [the offerings], one should meditate upon the *bālāgni* (the infant fire) as having the form of the infant fire, with a body of golden hue, six eyes and faces, and two sets of seven tongues;
[one should also meditate upon] the production of the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyapātra*), the jar, the spear, the discus, the mace, the *tomara*, and so forth.

Having worshipped Bālāgni with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bālāgni," one should take the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with their openings facing upward and then downward, perform the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*), and touch the roots, middles, and tips of the *sruk* and *sruva* individually with the roots, middles, and tips of *darbha* grass— representing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra respectively— and then rotate them over the fire in the *darbha*-fire.

Having removed [the thread] from the base to the end of the feet, consecrated it at those respective locations with the root-mantra of that deity, and having placed it upon *kuśa* grass on the left side,
one should worship Śiva and Śakti above those two, encircle it with a three-stranded thread while reciting the *kavaca* mantra, and then perform the meditation (*dhyāna*).
The *sṛk* and *sṛva* are the two cavities of the faces of Śakti and Śambhu, whose essential nature is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
Their tip is the *nādānta-nāda*, the state consisting of nectar, the root of food and the eater.

Having meditated thus: "The auspicious vessel, purified by mantras, possessing a stalk of the sun and moon, with a beautiful lotus-base, its fragrant essence produced from the stalk of the navel, beginningless"— having placed the pot upon the upper girdle on the left side and having performed the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*) as before, [one should place it] near the navel.
Having placed something above [the vessel] for the purpose of purification, having ignited the tip of a *darbha* blade, and having circled the clarified butter (*ājya*) and cast it into the fire;

then, having thrown two *darbha* tips into the clarified butter with the *astra-mantra*, and having placed the *ājya-sthālī* above the navel, one should unite it with the fire. Thereafter, for the sake of the oblation, one should perform the *atidhāvana*, *atiśravaṇa*, and so forth, upon oneself.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, with their respective mantras,
one should place a vessel of ghee on the right, the north-east, and the navel region using the tips of *darbha* grass, and then offer oblations with the tip of a *kuśa* blade.

Having placed a *pavitraka* made of two *darbha* blades— one span in length with a knot in the middle— into the midst of the clarified butter, one should perform the sprinkling (*āplavana*) over the left and right [sides] with the *hṛdaya* and *astra* mantras.
Having grasped the tips and roots together with the two thumbs and little fingers, one should perform three sprinklings as before;

then, having sprinkled [the materials] with the *astra* mantra, divided them into three parts with the *astra*, and untied the knot of the *pavitra*, one should sprinkle it with the *arghya* water and cast it into the fire.

For the sake of the *pavitra* preparation, having kindled the fire with a single blade of *darbha* using the *astra* mantra, one should gaze upon and circumambulate the vessels containing the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the sacrificial offerings (*havir-dravya*).

One should cast [the offering] into the fire; then, having established the *pavitra* made of two *darbha* blades in the midst of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having conceived the clarified butter as the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* channels, one should visualize the fire facing oneself with the root mantra. Then, grasping the *sruva* ladle with the *astra* mantra and the deer-gesture (*mṛgamudrā*), one [offers] with the *sruva* into the southern part of the clarified butter.

Having taken clarified butter from the left side, one offers it into the right eye of the fire with "Oṃ agnaye svāhā"; having taken clarified butter from the middle part, one offers it into the left eye of the fire with "Oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā"; having taken clarified butter from the middle part, one offers it into the middle eye of the fire with "Oṃ hāṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā";
and having offered it into the mouth of the fire with "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā" and "svāhā," [one proceeds] during the dark fortnight.
Saying "Oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā," one takes clarified butter from the left side into the fire’s left eye; saying "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā," one takes it from the center into the fire’s right eye.

Reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni, Soma, and Agni," one offers oblation into the central eye of the fire; then, reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" into the mouth of the fire as before, and having offered with "svāhā," one should mix the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*) with more clarified butter—this is the purification of the clarified butter for both the bright and dark fortnights. Having consecrated it again with the *saṃhitā* mantra, performed the binding of the directions and the sprinkling around the pit (*avakuṇḍana*), rendered it nectarine by means of the *surabhi-mudrā*, and consecrated it with the root mantra, [one should worship] with the heart mantra.

Having performed the purification of the clarified butter by pouring drops of ghee, one should then offer a single oblation with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ sadyojātāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ vāmadevāya svāhā*, *oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā*, *oṃ hoṃ īśānāya svāhā*. (Third line)
Line 1):

*Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ* to Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva, *svāhā*. *Oṃ hīṃ huṃ* to Vāmadeva and Aghora, *svāhā*. Line 4): *Oṃ huṃ heṃ* to Aghora and Tatpuruṣa, *svāhā*. *Oṃ heṃ hoṃ* to Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, *svāhā*. With these oblations... Line 5).

Having formed a union by joining the faces, one should perform the unification of the faces (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*) by offering oblations with the *sruva* ladle from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, from Agni to Vāyu, and from Nairṛti to Īśāna, saying "Svāhā"; then,
for the purpose of naming, one should worship [the deity] with Īśāna.

Having offered three oblations with the Astra-mantra and given the name "O Śiva-fire, you are the consumer of oblations," one should worship the Mother and Father of the Fire with the Hṛdaya-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, honor them with flowers, and dismiss them. Then, for the purpose of establishing the tongues, having offered oblations beginning with Hiraṇya and ending with Bahurūpa in the directions— east, south, west, north, northeast, southwest, and the center— one should perform the union of the faces as before.

Gradually, having offered oblations ending with *svāhā* using the seed-syllable *oṃ hūṃ*, one should visualize the unification of the tongues [of the deities]. Then, from the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) by the Lord of Sacrifice up to the end of the marriage rite, one should perform the ritual actions as prescribed for the sacraments (*saṃskāra*). For the sake of those rites, having offered three oblations for each part with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*), [one should prepare] the area as large as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

(4th line) Having formed the mental resolve as desired, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* using the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles upon the middle of the tongue, as previously described.

(5th line) Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should cast the clarified butter from the *sruc* and *sruva* into the fire in a stream the thickness of a barley grain. Thus, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*:

Having sat down, having sprinkled water around the fire, having worshipped with the root mantra and the Śivāsaṃhitā mantra, having worshipped the [sacrificial wood] taken from the Palāśa tree, having invoked [the deity], having displayed the previous mudrā, and having fully worshipped the fire with the Brahma-aṅgas;
He is in a state of meditation, with tawny limbs, three eyes, and adorned with a crown of matted locks;
on his right side he holds a rosary and a staff, and is beautified by *dūrvā* grass and a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*). (8th line)

Having meditated thus upon the God— who is seated upon the bull-throne, wears a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), is clothed in a tiger-skin garment, maintains the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*), and possesses the form of an elder— and having worshipped the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇa*) and offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and other substances to the deities of the enclosure and so forth, one should offer three oblations (*tri-āhuti*).

Having sprinkled water around the fire with the root mantra, and having offered sixteen oblations together with clarified butter as the sacrificial substance, one should offer three oblations with the *astra* mantra for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then offer the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and then offer the *sampāta* oblation. Having worshipped the deities of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and gathered the supporting fuel-sticks (*ādhārasamit*) and so forth along with the enclosing sticks, one should cast them into the fire. Then, having fully worshipped Indra and the other deities and presented the offering (*bali*), one should perform the inner and outer *bali* offerings.
