Having given [the offerings], dismissed the deities, sprinkled water around the fire, gathered the surrounding grass (*paristaraṇa*), and sprinkled [everything] with *arghya* water;

having dismissed the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and burned the darbha grass in the fire according to the procedure for the removal of defects (*lopakārya*); having lifted the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyapātra*) with the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons and offered an oblation with the root mantra;

having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) and displayed the gesture of salutation with joined palms (*namaskārāñjalimudrā*) to Agni; and having offered incense, lamps, and *arghya*, [one places it] upon the cooking pot (*sthālī*).
Having taken hold of the protection, having grasped the form of the fire with the root mantra, and having applied the protection,
[one should proceed] with the sounds of auspiciousness.
Having approached the presence of the deity with all musical instruments and attendants, having offered a handful of flowers with mantras upon the head of the deity,

having applied [the protective mark] on the forehead, having worshipped with the limbs of Brahmā, having offered incense, lamps, and water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), and likewise having had the Lord of All maintain it, one should perform the protection together with the Brahmins at the well-adorned site; [this is the rule for the daily fire-ritual].
[The Ritual for the Eternal Festival] (nityotsavavidhiḥ): The preceptor (ācārya),

together with his attendants, having approached the presence [of the deity] as prescribed in the ritual for the bali offering, shall sprinkle the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya) with the Astra-mantra.

Having worshipped the seat and performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should perform the installation (*sthāpana*) as before, display the mudrās, offer incense, lamps, and the water-offering (*arghya*), and perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Having adorned the deity with fragrant garlands, ornaments, and so forth, and having placed the deity upon the colored powder (*raṅga*), one should attach all the ritual substances to the seat, worship the seat as before, and worship the Vāyavya-Gāyatrī.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* and the other *kalās* as before, and having worshipped the Śakti, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[He has] a right hand, three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
In his left hand he holds a supreme vessel of nectar, and in his right, an axe and the gesture of fearlessness.
The god, beautiful in all his limbs, wears a tiger-skin as an upper garment;
he holds Umā in his left [arm], has three eyes, and is adorned with a crown containing a casket.
Having meditated thus upon the Goddess, who stands in the *tribhaṅga* posture with her lower garment [adorned] like a peacock feather,

and having worshipped her with the six limbs beginning with Īśāna, one should worship the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) in the second enclosure, and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the third enclosure. Having worshipped the Goddess as one does Gaurī, and having offered food (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*), one should again adorn her with garments, flower garlands, and so forth, and [perform] the worship of the parasol, fly-whisk, and canopy.

Having mounted the deity with incense, lamps, and all other ritual offerings along with the attendants, and having caused [the image] to circumambulate the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should take up the vessel for consecration (*abhiṣeka-pātra*) together with the attendant holding the oblation-ladle and the bell.

Having struck [the door] with the mantra *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, together with those who recite auspicious and benedictory words, one should place the prescribed [mudrā] with the middle finger of the right hand upon the lower stone of the door, and having placed a flower above it—

Having protected [the site] and displayed the *avakuṇṭhana* and other mudrās, one should collect [the materials] according to the following measurements: for the subtle [level], it is said to be equal to a peacock’s egg; for the medium, the fruit of the *mallikūca*; and for the small, the size of an *āmalaka*.
For the gods and the Gaṇapas, however, it should be five finger-breadths in circumference and circular in shape.

For the *bhūtas*, it should be long; for the *śaktis*, triangular; for the *munis*, [it should be] like a *muni* [in shape]; for the *yakṣas*, the size of a fist; for the *rākṣasas*, cart-shaped; for the *paiśācas*, the form of a trident; and for humans, by holding [the offering] with fingers, the measure of the *bali* is prescribed. Having taken it thus: *oṃ hāṃ vighnāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ vighneśvarāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ vighnarājāya*... (4th line).
Having offered the bali with "svāhā," [one offers] to the right: "oṃ hāṃ daṇḍine svāhā," and to the north: "oṃ hāṃ muṇḍine svāhā" inside.
(5th line)

At the head of the bull, having offered *oṃ hāṃ vṛṣabhāya svāhā* and on its back everywhere *sarvatra bhūtāya svāhā*, [he offers] to the south *oṃ hāṃ kuṇḍodarabhūtāya svāhā*, and to the south of that *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇyadevyai svāhā*, and [to] Caṇḍikādevī *svāhā*.

Having offered the final *bali*, one offers a *bali* to Vīrabhadra and Vighneśvara with the mantra "svāhā" to the east and west of that [central deity]. To the southwest, a *bali* is offered to Dīrghabhūta with "svāhā.
To the west of that, to Mahāgaṇapati with "svāhā. On the roof of the temple (*vimāna*), to Hrasvadevabhūta with "svāhā. To the northwest, to Siṃhabhūtarūpa with "svāhā."
To the one who has become a cave in its western direction, svāhā; to Jyeṣṭhā in its eastern direction, svāhā; to the one who has become elephant-faced in its northern direction, svāhā;

to Durgā in its southern direction, svāhā; to Sūrya in its eastern direction, svāhā; to the one who has become Brahmā in the northeast, svāhā—having thus offered the second *bali*, [one offers] to Āmoda in the south and north of that door in the second enclosure, svāhā.

Having offered as before at the front of the second bull with "To Pramoda, Svāhā! (6th line), and having announced the offerings of incense, lamps, sacred texts, knowledge, song, instrumental music, and so forth for Indra with "To Indra, Svāhā!", one should offer the *bali* as far as Īśāna,
and then [offer] to its south (7th line).

"Kṣetrapālāya svāhā"—this concludes the half of the third enclosure. Again, in the third enclosure, having offered oblations thus: "Viṣṇave svāhā" in the southwest (Nairṛta) and "Brahmaṇe svāhā" in the northeast (Aiśānī), one should lead the image to the eastern side of the *bhūtapīṭha* facing north, wash the pedestal with water, and [place it] upon a white lotus (*kumuda*).

Having worshipped the deities beginning with Indra in the eight directions, one should offer salutations upon the lintel (*paṭṭikā*) as follows: in the northern region, "Salutation to Brahmā"; between Brahmā and Īśāna;
in the middle [of the lintel], "Salutation to the Ādityas"; between Īśāna and Indra, "Salutation to Bhāskara-Kṣetrapāla"; and between Indra and Agni, "Salutation to the hosts of Apsarases."

Having worshipped with "Salutation to the Munis between Vāyu and Varuṇa," "Salutation to the Vasus between Vāyu and Soma," and "Salutation to the Rudras between Soma and Īśāna," one should then worship outside the pedestal: first, "Salutation to the hosts of Piśācas" in the east, and "Salutation to the hosts of Yakṣas" in the south.

"Obeisance to the Rakṣasas in the west; obeisance to the Gandharvas in the north; obeisance to the Bhūtas in the northeast. Having thus worshipped, one should worship the eight Śaktis upon the eight petals above.
In the center of the pericarp: "Obeisance to Avighna. On the eastern petal: "Obeisance to Āmoda. On the southern [petal]: "Obeisance to Pramoda. On the western petal... [F33b]

(First line) Having worshipped with "Salutation to Pramukha" on the northern petal and "Salutation to Vimukha," [one worships] likewise with "Salutation to the Gods," ending with "namaḥ. (Second line)

Having offered the *bali* with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*, and having offered a food *bali* in the center measuring the size of a coconut, one should announce all the ritual services (*upacāra*). Then, having worshipped the deity again with the root mantra and performed the worship of the sandals (*pādukārcana*), [this is the procedure for offering the *bali*]. On the secondary pedestal (*upapīṭha*) is [the deity] surrounded by the eight *nāgas*, the elephant, and the pair of wind-gods.

Kumuda, Bhūtarūpa, and Kuṇḍarākṣasa; and it is said that the upper frieze is adorned with the hundred Rudras. It has five faces, with equal mouths, noses, and eyes; ten necks, ten arms, ten tridents, and ten throats; a single heart; and an exceedingly red complexion with two feet.
Thus is the form of the sacrificial pedestal for the *bhūtas*.
Āmoda, Pramoda, Pramukha, Vimukha, Vimukha,
and likewise Avighna and Vighnakartā— these six are the leaders of the *bhūtas*.
In the *daivika* [balis], [the offering] belongs to Bhava and the others; in the *mānuṣa*, to Indra and the others;
in the *svayambhūta*, to the *bhūtas* and the others; in the *ārṣa*, however, it belongs to the *pariṣad*.
In the *bāṇaliṅga*, it belongs to the Vasus; and in the *rākṣasa*, to the Yakṣas and the others.
One should offer an oblation (*bali*) to Anantadivyaliṅga and to Saptaliṅga.
Devalī, Balibhava, Śatadhā, Īśāna, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhīma, Mahādeva, and Aṣṭamūrti— these are remembered as the eight forms.
The offering for the human-liṅga is for Indra and the others; the offering for the self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga is supreme.

In the eastern part of the womb [of the mandala], one should place Caturmukha in the southeast, Kuṇḍodara in the south, Suprabha in the southwest, Siṃhavaktra in the west, and Adhomukha in the northwest.
One should offer Soma and Ekapāda with their desired feet in the northeast;
these are the offerings one should cast as a *bali* for the retinue of the eight Bhūtas,
as well as for the Ṛṣis, Liṅgas, Bali, Vṛṣa, Nandīdhara, and Śaktiva.
Brahmā and the others, Śakti, Gaṇapa, Kumāra, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, Dharaṇījayanta, Śrī Nīlarudra, and the bali at the site of the balipīṭha; the asatva-bāṇaliṅga-bali:
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, and Anala.
Pratyuṣas and Prabheśa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
The offering for the *liṅga* of the Rākṣasas:
Ananteśa, as well as Sūkṣma, Śivottama,
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin.

One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), fire oblations (*homa*), the worship of the retinue, and the offering of bali. One should worship during the three times or the eight times as prescribed for the *sandhyā* rites.
Regarding the measure of the bali offering, that which is performed on the full moon day (*bāhula*) is said to be the best; the medium [measure] is also prescribed.
A mere handful is said to be the lowest; thus the *svāhuti* is described, and this is called the *bali*. Now, for the worship of the sandals (*pādukā*):

having placed [the sandals] upon a vessel, having worshipped the seat, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamp, and water for honor (*arghya*), one should invoke [the deity], adorn [it] with a seat and so forth, as well as garments, garlands, and ornaments, and [perform the rite] with its own mantra and the mantra of the bull (*vṛṣabha*).
Having performed the propitiation of the cloth, having worshipped it, protected it, and veiled it, one should display the great mudrā of the cloth-liṅga below.
As for the meditation:
[one should visualize the deity] resembling the pomegranate flower, with hair standing erect and three eyes. (5th line)
The god holds a noose and a goad, and has a trident and a white water-lily upon his head.
Adorned with white *arka* and jasmine flowers, wearing yellow garments, and bearing [the insignia],
one should meditate upon and contemplate the Lord described as being in the form of sandals (*pādukā*).
Having meditated thus, having performed worship, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and the water of honor (*arghya*),

the preceptor (*ācārya*) places [the image] upon the head of an attendant; then, together with all musical instruments and ritual services, he places it before the deity and [proceeds] with the mantras along with flowers.

Having cast away the water from the *pulaka* [offering], one should recite: *Oṃ hāṃ, O you who are the secret of secrets, because you are the protector (*goptṛ*), accept this rite performed here; may success be mine through your grace, for you abide within me.*

Oṃ hāṃ! Whatever action there may be, O Lord, whether well-done or ill-done, consume and destroy that for me in the state of Śiva, O Śaṅkara! Oṃ hāṃ! Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world. Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; he who is Śiva, I am indeed He.
One should offer a handful of water (*culukodaka*) into the left hand of Śiva; one should offer oneself, the recitation (*japa*), and the ritual action (*karman*) into his right hand.
Thus it is stated as a specific rule regarding the cause:
"The *añjali* [gesture] is in the right hand, and the *kūjita* [sound]."
Or, having taken a flower four finger-breadths in size, one should offer it at the base of the feet.
This is declared to be the "handful of water" (culukodaka) which arises at the conclusion of the worship.
O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, remain present within this *liṅga* with a spirit of affection until the conclusion of the worship.

Having thus made the request with the mantra, and having worshipped the deity with eight flowers while saying "Forgive me" (*kṣamasva*) using the root mantra—[it is taught that] the flower-liṅga is for the morning time, the food-liṅga for midday, and the unbroken grain (*akṣata*) liṅga for the evening; these are proclaimed as the [three] times for the liṅga. Having worshipped upon the pedestal with the root mantra and having honored it with Pāśupata [mantra], one should offer the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, along with incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and the water of honor (*arghya*).
Having meditated [upon him] as four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with a crown of matted hair;
It is joined with a golden ring and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.

Having meditated thus: "Wearing a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and adorned with white garlands," one should worship the *saṃhitā*s. Then, having purified the vessel with a cloth and having turned inward, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) along with the root mantra to Niśākara Vṛṣabheśvara.
Having joined with Skanda at midday, one should again join him with water for the pleasure of the deity, as stated by Bharata.
(6th line) Having caused a pure dance to be performed, the preceptor should duly perform circumambulation, prostration, hymns of praise, and recitation before the form of Śiva and the deities.
(7th line) Having worshipped the Liṅga-deity in its former place with flowers, having offered the *nirodha-arghya*, and having drawn the curtain, he should go outside. (F36a, 1st line)

Having performed the *caṇḍapūjā* in the temple of Caṇḍeśvara, one should bring the *nirmālya*, place it before [the deity], and sprinkle the image of Caṇḍa with pure water. Then, having worshipped the seat with "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Dhvanicaṇḍa," and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), and so forth as prescribed, one should display the mudrās, adorn [the deity] with garments, perfumes, garlands, and the like, and having fully embellished and worshipped [him].
Dhyāna has two eyes, is yellow in color, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair;
he holds an axe in his right hand and raises his left hand upward.
With the right leg extended and the left leg resting,
[he holds] the sacrificial thread, ornaments, and the great lord Caṇḍeśa.

Having meditated thus, one should worship with "To Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara, *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*," worship the limbs (*aṅga*), offer the deity's remains (*nirmālya*) along with water for drinking, betel, and so forth, and having obtained permission, one should offer the *arghya* with the root-mantra of Caṇḍa; then, again with the root-mantra, having performed a salutation with "To the Heart, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*," one offers the *arghya* facing away.

Having given [the offerings] and dismissed [the deity], and having again performed the *caṇḍāṣṭaka* hymn, prostrations, and so forth, as well as the recitation (*japa*) of the root mantra according to one's capacity, one should clasp the hands together while reciting:
"O Caṇḍeśvara, grant the fruit of the worship of Śambhu, whose mind is agitated by the words 'Nīlakaṇṭha'; salutations to you! Thus is the hand-clasp (*karavaṣpoṭya*).
Having performed the prayer [thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of Caṇḍa].

Then, rising at dawn during the Manonmanī-pūjā, having meditated upon one’s own Guru, Gaṇeśa, and the worship of Śiva, one should perform the evacuation of waste, the cleaning of the teeth, the ash-bath, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), and so forth.
(Second line) Having arranged [the ritual space], washed his feet, and sipped water (ācamana), he enters the abode of Manonmanī. At the entrance, facing north, he prepares a beautiful seat.

(Third line) Having applied the *tripuṇḍra* mark and performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he performs the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) by reciting: (Fourth line) "Oṃ hāṃ, to the weapon [mantra]. Thus it is said.

Having cleansed the palms and backs of the hands and having sprinkled them with water using the *Śakti* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: *Saying:* "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Manonmanī," [one places it on the palms].

*Saying:* "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Manonmanī," one should place the thumbs upon the little fingers of both hands. Then, with the two index fingers upon the two thumbs: *Saying:* "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart," [one places it] on the little, ring, and middle fingers. *Saying:* "Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the head. *Saying:* "Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). *Saying:* "Oṃ haiṃ, salutation to the armor (*kavaca*)."
Homage! (7th line) With the middle fingers of both palms:
*oṃ hrūṃ* homage to the eyes; with the two index fingers: *oṃ aḥ* homage to the weapon (*astra*). (F37b, 1st line)

Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) and protected [the body] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), having joined [the hands], and having placed the seat, form, and mantra-mantras in the heart, one should place [the mantras] on the right thumb, little finger, and so forth;

on the heart, head, and crest; on the two breasts with the middle fingers; on the space between those two with the index fingers; on the three eyes with the three [mantras]; and perform the triple-clapping and the binding of the directions.
Having enveloped [the disciple] with the Vajrakavaca armor and performed the rite for the removal of evil by means of the root mantra,
one should contemplate oneself in the form of Manonmani. Thereafter, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*),

and having first executed the placement of the digits of the Mother (*mātṛkalānyāsa*) and the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should wash the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) using the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having filled [the vessel] with the Heart mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, having worshipped it with the root mantra of the form of Manonmanī and its limbs (*aṅga*), and having performed the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*nirikṣaṇa*),

one should consecrate the substance with the root mantra and its limbs, perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and so forth, display the cow’s teat (*gostanī*) and womb (*yoni*) mudrās,
and [sprinkle] the substance with the water of the *arghya* using the Astra mantra.

Having sprinkled water and consecrated it with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), one should duly worship oneself, the seat, and the image with the root mantra; then, having recited the root mantra and proclaimed the *puṇyāha* (day of merit), one should prepare the *pañcagavya* and worship Vighneśvara at the archway, above the door, and in the right, left, and middle [sections].
Having worshipped Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī fashioned [therein] on the right and left sides of the door, Gaṅgā and Yoginī on the left and right of the left side of the door,

Yamunā and Ḍākinī on the two right door-panels, and Sindhu and Godāvarī on the lower door-jamb at the front of the altar, as well as the bull; and having warded off the three obstacles with the root-mantra, the Astra-mantra, and the Pāśupata-astra, he should take his station slightly to the left of the doorway.

Having entered with the right foot foremost, one should worship the door-keeper at the threshold, saying: *oṃ hāṃ astrāya dvārapālāya namaḥ*. Then, having worshipped the Vāstu-Brahmā in the southwest and Manonmanī with the Gāyatrī of Gaurī, and having offered incense, lamps, and the water-offering (*arghya*), one should cast away the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*) and again worship Manonmanī with the Gāyatrī of Gaurī.

Having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, and having discarded the *nirmālya*, one should worship Manonmanī with the Gaurī-gāyatrī, offer incense, lamps, and *arghya*, purify the image with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, worship the seat (*āsana*), perform the purification, and establish the fourfold foundation beginning with Ādhāra-śakti and Ananta.
Having worshipped the lower and upper covers, one should worship Keśava— who consists of the unmanifest, necessity, the constituent parts, and time— within the four-footed center of the pair;
and having worshipped the four lotuses, which consist of the bulb, seed, sprout, stalk, filaments, and pericarp, as the seats for the four mandalas in the midst of the four Kālikās.
Having invoked the form [of the deity],
[one should place] on the head, the eyes, the heart, the throat, the two arms, the hips, the private parts, the thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, and the feet.

On the sides, feet, and the two breasts are Tārā, Vidyā, Mṛtyuśuddhā, Ajara, Medhā, Svadhā, Svasti, Bālinī, Jvālinī, Kṛṣṇā, Dhṛti, Kāmā, Mati, Prajācintā, Bhūmi, Kṣayā, Śāntā, Vāmadeva, Kalā, Umā, Śānti, Dānti, Dayā, Sūti, Savya, and Sadyojāta.
Having placed the twenty-five *kalās*, having visualized the eyes of the *vidyā*-body, and having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, one should offer the invocation (*āvāhana*),

stabilization (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), intense presence (*sannirodhana*), welcome (*svāgata*), and the water for honor (*arghya*). Then, having applied the eyes and the heart and other limbs (*aṅgas*) starting from the head and the bath (*snāna*) to the eyes and the rest.

Having performed the ritual binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and so forth, and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the guest-offering (*arghya*) with mantras ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*, one should bathe [the deity] with oil massage (*abhyaṅga*), fragrant unguents (*udvartana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and so on,
as well as with scented water (*gandhāmbu*). Then, having offered water for sipping and the guest-offering once more, one should wipe [the deity] dry with a fine cloth.

Having adorned [the deity] with garments, perfumes, crowns, bracelets, armlets, incense, garlands, and so forth, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) along with the root mantra, and having presented the *arghya* water,

one should display the *dhenupadmayoni* mudrās and pray for the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅgapūjā*). In the first enclosure, [one worships] in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Nairṛti, and Vāyu.
At the bases of the eastern petals are Dayā and the others, numbering five; those are the limbs (*aṅga*) in the four directions of the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*).
In the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*), starting from the east and extending to the northeast in the four directions, are Śubhāśubhavatī, Vijayā, and Sumālinī.
In the fourth enclosure, having worshipped the powers beginning with Vāmā in the eight directions, and Brahmā, Bhṛṅgin, Vīrabhadra, and Vighneśvara in the [directions] of Īśāna and Nairṛta;

and in the fifth enclosure, having worshipped Vṛṣabha, Vināyaka, Sṛṣṭi, Skanda, Śanaiścara, Kṣetrapāla, and Bhāskara in the directions beginning with the East, and having offered the *arghya*, one should present a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Goddess with the root mantra, as well as *arghya*, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*).

Having offered water for drinking, water for rinsing the mouth, betel leaves, and so forth, one should present the *parivāra-bali* at the right and left door-panels; in front [of them], the *Śaṅkhanidhi*;
and in the directions starting from the east, Jambhinī, Stambhinī, Mohinī, Bhedinī, Ramaṇī, Bhadrakālī, Durgā, and Caṇḍeśvarī.

On the southern side of the gopura, at the Mahāpīṭha of Daṇḍimuṇḍī, in the four petals starting from the east and in the pericarp, [one should worship] Cakrāśemā, Agrabhūta, Mātruloka, Mātrideva, Mātṛrakta, and the Mothers. Having offered the bali preceded by the washing,

sprinkling, invocation, water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and mudrās, one should offer the arghya water with the heart-mantra in the añjali gesture.

One should offer water for the *arghya* and then, having entered the kitchen, perform the daily rites (*nityakarman*) by means of the *yonikuṇḍa*. Having approached the Goddess and presented incense, lamps, the *ārātrika*, ashes, a mirror, a parasol, chowries, and a fan, and having honored her with the *arghya* while reciting the Vedic hymns (*sūkta*) of the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas, one should announce one's knowledge through circumambulation and the recitation of ancient texts. Then, having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one’s capacity, [one should place it] in the left hand.
Having offered [the deity] with *arghya* water, having recited the *aṅga-mantras* ten times [their respective portions], and having worshipped [the deity] with the eightfold flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),

having offered *arghya* again, having performed circumambulation and prostration with the *astra-mantra*, and having said "Forgive me," having worshipped [the deity] with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*),

having offered the *arghya* for departure (*parāṅmukha-arghya*), and having raised the limbs [of the deity] with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should unite [the deity] with the image (*mūrti*) by means of the *mūrti-mantra*.

Having conceived of oneness with the *mūla* [mantra], having performed worship, and having carried out the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and other rites, one should withdraw the mantras for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. Then, having approached Caṇḍeśvarī, and having worshipped her with the *mūla* [mantras] while her hands hold the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), one should dismiss her. Then, having bathed that throne-form (*āsana-mūrti*), having worshipped it with the *mūla* and its limbs (*aṅga*), and having offered the water for the feet and so forth, one should present the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*). Having given the food offering (*naivedya*) and the water for the guest-offering, one should then offer the *arghya*.
[One should] withdraw [the mind]; thus is the procedure for worship in Manonmanī.
The characteristics of the daily festival worship are as follows:
(3rd line)

The water for the feet (*pādya*) destroys sins; the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) brings prosperity; the water of honor (*arghya*) ensures the success of one's actions; and the seat (*āsana*) increases one's progeny. Water is declared to be for pacification (*śāntika*); scented oil bestows happiness; the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are purifying; and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) lead to victory. Ghee bestows liberation; milk increases longevity; curd is said to increase offspring; and the sixth, honey, indeed releases one from debt. Turmeric brings the subjugation of kings.
The *ikṣusāra* destroys disease as well as impurity; honey brings health and becomes one's own essential nature (*svārasvata*).

The pomegranate (*dhāḍimī*) destroys anger, and the *kulaṃjī* fruit destroys grief. The *pañcāmṛta* likewise increases the harvest of plantains (*kadalī*). The breadfruit tree (*panasa*) [brings] the world... the mango (*āmra*)— [End of fragment]
All victory shall be attained; by [the mantra] one becomes a minister (*mantrin*). Likuca destroys death; Śakra destroys enemies; and the coconut grants [prosperity].
(Second line) Sālokya is attained through the essence of the *bilva* fruit; Sāmīpya through the worship of the mantra; Sārūpya through incense and lamps; and Sāyujya through fragrant water.
(Third line) Through the consecration with *kaṭanā*, there is good fortune.

The conquest of the quarters, the [offering of] snow-water, the garment that liberates from poverty, camphor that destroys the house [of sin], and the [offering of] *akṣata* which destroys [the cycle of] rebirth—these constitute merit in the worship of the conch. Washing [the conch] brings about the destruction of enemies;

burning incense burns away sins; the lamp is the destroyer of death; the lamp in a water-jar brings great peace; the *nīrājana* rite yields great fruit; and the sacred ash is for the protection of the three worlds.
The mirror bestows knowledge; the parasol grants kingship; the fly-whisk brings good fortune; and the sacrificial offering, as well as the palm-leaf fan, brings all auspicious splendor.
Singing, music, and instrumental performance increase the king’s kingdom. Having thus worshipped with auspicious rites at the conclusion—

One shall attain union (*sāyujya*). Whether at a Vedic site or within the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*), upon seeing or even touching [the deity], one should discard earthen vessels and perform the *mūrtihoma*.
Then, having performed the purification of the *liṅga*, one should consecrate it with ritual ablutions (*snapanas*).
